opus-5.5.text:
I think the key distinction is between *what* gets rewarded and *where* in the process the decision is made. People often hear "reinforcement learning for image generation" and picture one monolithic model being nudged toward prettier pictures. That's not really what's going on with these two.

With the Architect, the reinforcement learning operates at the level of structure and planning. Before any pixels exist, the model decides what the scene should contain: which objects, where they sit, how they relate spatially, and how the composition satisfies the prompt. The reward is about faithfulness and coherence. Did you put three cups on the table when the user asked for three? Is the dog actually to the left of the bicycle? Those are discrete, checkable decisions, and RL fits them well because you can define a fairly objective reward and let the policy explore different layouts.

The Artist works at the rendering level. It takes that plan and turns it into a convincing image: texture, lighting, style, fine detail. The reward there is softer and more perceptual. It reflects aesthetic quality, realism, and consistency with the intended style, and it often relies on learned preference models rather than hard rules. So the optimization looks different. You're shaping a distribution of visual qualities rather than verifying a set of constraints.

Separating the two matters because if you fold everything into one reward signal, the model finds shortcuts. It might produce a gorgeous image that quietly ignores half the prompt, because aesthetics dominate the reward. Or it gets the layout right but the image looks flat and synthetic. Decoupling them lets each stage optimize for the thing it's actually responsible for, and it makes failures much easier to diagnose. When something goes wrong you can ask whether it was a planning error or a rendering error, instead of staring at a single opaque score.

So the takeaway is that reinforcement learning isn't one knob here. It's applied with different objectives at different levels of abstraction, and that division of labor is a big part of why the combined system can be both controllable and visually strong.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think the key distinction is between what the reinforcement learning is actually optimizing in each case, because they're really doing two different jobs.

With the Architect, the RL is operating at the level of planning. So the model isn't being rewarded for pretty pixels, it's being rewarded for producing a good structural blueprint for the image: the layout, where the objects go, how they relate spatially, whether the composition actually satisfies the constraints in the prompt. The reward signals there are things like, did you get the count right, is the object on the left actually on the left, are the attributes bound to the correct entities. It's much closer to the kind of verifiable, almost symbolic reward you see in reasoning-style RL for language models.

The Artist is the opposite end. There the RL is about rendering and aesthetics, so the reward is coming from human preference or learned reward models that capture realism, style, texture, how visually appealing the output is. That's inherently a softer, more subjective signal, and it has all the usual reward-hacking pitfalls where the model learns to produce oversaturated, overly smooth images that score well but don't look like what people actually want.

And the reason I think that separation matters is that if you try to do both with a single reward, they fight each other. Aesthetic rewards tend to pull you away from faithfully following awkward or unusual prompts, and strict compositional rewards don't care at all whether the image looks good. So decoupling them lets you use the right kind of RL for the right kind of problem: hard, checkable rewards for the structure, and preference-based rewards for the appearance. The Artist is essentially conditioned on the Architect's plan, so it gets to focus entirely on execution without having to re-solve the compositional reasoning. That's the distinction I'd want people to hold onto.

astra-6.text: The important distinction is between using reinforcement learning to train the model and using a trained model to generate an image. Those are different stages. A reward can guide learning toward outputs that better satisfy an objective, but that does not necessarily mean the model is running a reinforcement-learning loop every time it produces an image. For Architect and Artist, we should ask what each model controls, what receives the reward, and when that feedback is applied. Their names alone don’t establish those details.
